Seoul braces for heatwave sweeping South Korea as death toll reaches 16
Trucks are dousing capital’s roads with water and nurses are checking on vulnerable people as heat heads westwards
Seoul is bracing for its first ever “severe heatwave warning” on Tuesday, as South Korea reels from a deadly heatwave that has seen the country record its highest ever temperature.
The south-eastern city of Yangsan reached an all-time national record of 42.5C on Sunday afternoon – the highest temperature measured in 122 years of weather observations – and now the heat is shifting westwards, approaching the densely populated capital of more than 9 million people, which is forecast to hit 38C on Tuesday followed by three sweltering days of 37C.
South Korea has recorded 16 fatalities linked to heat and more than 2,000 people treated for heat-related illnesses since May, according to the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.
Speaking at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, President Lee Jae Myung called on officials to take necessary measures to protect the daily lives of people and inspect power systems as demand for airconditioning surges.
“We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system, since this extreme weather is becoming normal,” he said.
Seoul authorities held an emergency meeting on Monday and launched initiatives to counter the heat and alleviate health risks. It is the first time the capital has seen a severe heatwave warning under a new system established this year as the government sought to improve how it responds to rising temperatures.
Nurses are conducting checks on up to 63,000 residents deemed most vulnerable, including elderly people and people with disabilities or chronic illnesses.
In an attempt to dampen rising urban heat in Seoul, a fleet of 200 trucks are spraying almost 2,000km of roads with water. The trucks are operating up to six times a day in the most problematic areas.
Seoul’s pedestrian commuters have been snaking their way to work through patches of shade, avoiding direct sunlight even in the morning’s cooler early hours. Others have sought relief under mist-spray zones around the city.
Elsewhere, officials in North Gyeongsang province are flying drones equipped with loudspeakers to broadcast safety messages. The drones are also using thermal imaging cameras over areas crowded with people on summer holidays.
The nation’s highest temperature on Monday was 41.2C in Goryeong. Multiple cities and regions topped 41C and Seoul reached 39C in the Guro district.
Outdoor workers are bearing the brunt of the oppressive heat. A construction worker in Seoul, identified by the Korea Times only as Kim, said: “We take a 10-minute break every hour, but there isn’t even a fan here, so all we can do is sit in the shade … I sweat so much that my clothes rub my skin raw wherever they touch.”
Lee, a 55-year-old from Gwangmyeong who collects shopping carts in a supermarket car park, said conditions were brutal. “Lacking ventilitation makes the experience feel like being inside a sauna.” Concern has been expressed for food delivery riders.
The Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) has attributed the heatwave to overlapping high-pressure systems over the Korean peninsula combined with strong, direct sunlight under clear skies.
The heat in South Gyeongsang province, in the south-east, has been intensified by the “foehn phenomenon” – which occurs when wind crosses a mountain range and becomes hotter and drier on the other side.
Another factor in the heatwave mix is Typhoon Dolphin, which has the potential to make conditions better or worse, depending on its path.
If the typhoon moves towards eastern China, it could increase humidity and potentially worsening the heatwave and tropical nights in Korea, the KMA said. But a path closer to the south of the peninsula could bring stronger winds, greater cloud cover and rain, temporarily easing the heat.
As of Monday, Dolphin was continuing westwards towards the Japanese island of Okinawa, south of the Korean peninsula. It is forecast to weaken further and make landfall as a category 1 or 2 typhoon.
Scientists warn that extreme weather events such as heatwaves are becoming more frequent and intense as a result of human-induced climate change.

Three lions have died at a Tokyo zoo and several more have fallen ill, most likely due to extreme heat, following several weeks of record-breaking temperatures across Japan.
The park’s lion exhibit had been suspended since July 23 after several of the big cats showed signs of sickness, such as loss of appetite, fatigue and decreased activity, in mid-July, Tokyo’s Tama Zoo said in a statement Monday.
The three lions that died were all female: Mugi, age 3, Ichigo, age 11, and Luena, age 15. The zoo had a total of 16 lions, including five males, as of July 18.

Extreme heat costs poorest workers their health and wages
When temperatures soar across Asia's cities, informal workers face a choice: risk their health or lose their income. For many, the effects don't end when the workday is over.
Brijpal Singh spends long hours working construction under the blazing sun in Noida, a sprawling industrial satellite city in India’s National Capital Region. Even as temperatures soar past 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit), work on the building site rarely stops.
By the end of each shift, the 51-year-old says his heart is pounding, and he’s usually dizzy, dehydrated and physically drained from hours in the heat. Yet taking a day off is a luxury he cannot afford.
Missing work would mean losing his daily wage of 500 to 600 rupees ($6 to $7, €5.20 to €6.10). The money supports his wife and three children living in a village in Uttar Pradesh, a two-day journey away .
Article continues after this advertisement
“There are days when I don’t feel like working,” said Singh. “But if I miss a day, who will take care of my children and pay for their expenses?”
Some 5 million people work in the Delhi region’s informal economy, accounting for roughly 80% of the total workforce. And as climate change drives up temperatures, many paid by the day like Singh are faced with an impossible trade-off between providing for their families and protecting their health.
Extreme heat harms health, productivity and earnings
The past decade has been India’s warmest on record, bringing more frequent, intense, and prolonged heat waves. At the same time, heat is reducing productivity and increasing illnesses, with one study finding rising temperatures could be costing informal workers the equivalent of 2% of their country’s GDP annually. That’s nearly $80 billion (€69 billion).
“Wage losses are only going to worsen as temperatures continue to rise,” said Ameena Kidwai, lead researcher at People’s Courage International, a nonprofit aiming to strengthen informal workers’ rights. “Workers are now putting in many more hours than they did before to complete the same amount of work.”
The US-based organization surveyed informal workers in five Asian cities. Kidwai said some of those surveyed reported that tasks once completed in eight hours now take 10 to 12 hours during the hottest months, as they slow down to cope with dangerous conditions.
Article continues after this advertisement
With heat becoming a major occupational hazard, workers described the harm to their health, ranging from respiratory and gastrointestinal illnesses to stroke and kidney disease.
“As a result, workers also have to spend more on over-the-counter medicines and visits to clinics or hospitals,” Kidwai said.
Out of the work frying pan and into the home furnace
A lack of ability to recover is a defining feature of urban heat for informal workers — from construction laborers and street vendors to delivery riders — say researchers.
Like Singh, many are migrants who leave their families behind to earn a living in fast-growing cities, said Patricia Samantha Narvaez, a program manager at the Philippine development organization IDEALS.
“You would expect home to be a place of relief,” said Narvaez. “But many live in densely packed neighborhoods with poor ventilation, little green space and heat-absorbing concrete.”
That’s the case for Singh, who returns to a single room with poor ventilation after work. During the hot months from April to June, it becomes a furnace, and frequent power cuts make it difficult to cool down before the next day’s shift.
“During the hot days, I can’t eat well,” Singh said. “I often drink oral rehydration solution and go to bed without eating.”
Narvaez surveyed informal workers in Quezon City for a report on the impacts of extreme heat. The city is just northeast of Manila, the capital of the Philippines, a country in which some 42% of the employed population are informal workers.
“Some participants described Quezon City as a ‘concrete jungle’ because even at night it remains unbearably hot,” said Narvaez.
Fifty-year-old Aida Tano has experienced such conditions firsthand. Tano worked in a garment factory in Quezon City for nearly two decades, where soaring temperatures, heat-generating machinery and poor ventilaton turned the production floor into an oven. With no air conditioning, four workers shared one electric fan.
“There was no escape from the heat,” Tano said. “We complained, but management told us that if we couldn’t endure it, we could leave.”
Narvaez says it’s not unusual for factory owners to restrict measures that help workers cope with the heat even for trivial reasons such as not wanting fans to break down. At Tano’s workplace, she had to pay for her own drinking water, and even climbing stairs to leave on her break became too exhausting in the heat.
The factory has since closed, but after a long day in extreme heat, Tano, who now does odd jobs like sewing and cleaning, would come back to a house with no AC. She still relies on electric fans and keeping windows covered to block the sun, both of which do little to cool her home.
Working women bear the brunt of extreme heat
The economic impacts of climate change hit women hardest, largely because they account for a majority of the world’s poor, according to the United Nations.
Women in the informal economy also shoulder a disproportionately large burden because they combine paid work with unpaid caregiving responsibilities, said Ameena Kidwai of People’s Courage International.
“They’re managing their jobs while also running their households,” Kidwai said. “When children or older family members fall sick during a heat wave, the caregiving duties falls largely on women.”
Shanti Devi, a 36-year-old daily wage laborer in Noida, has been her family’s sole breadwinner since her husband was injured in a workplace accident several years ago.
“Now I have to manage the house, care for my children and also try to earn a living,” said Devi.
During heat waves, school closures and a shift to online classes often force Devi to stay home with her four children instead of going to work. Each day of lost wages adds to the already struggling family’s financial strain.
“I took the day off because it is too hot to work, and my children are home because their school is closed for the summer,” Devi said. “I have to cook for them. When school is open, they eat their meals there.”
Frequent power outages and overheated homes, also leave many women up through the night caring for family members in the heat before returning to work the next day. Disrupted sleep and lack of rest come with increased health risks, such as heart disease and diabetes, meaning women are often more vulnerable than men in heat waves.
Researchers say these overlapping pressures expose a gap in many cities’ efforts to adapt to a heating planet. While India has introduced heat action plans, and Quezon City is developing its own measures, protections for informal workers remain limited and unevenly enforced.
As temperatures rise because of human-caused climate change, experts say measures focus largely on short-term responses and often overlook the realities of informal workers’ lives.

Thunderstorm and flash flood warning as latest heatwave comes to an end
Flash flooding could hit in areas with ground scorched by the recent heatwaves
Bookmark
Bookmark popover
Removed from bookmarks
Heavy rain could hit parts of the UK today during the final day of the latest sweltering heatwave.
There are thunderstorm warning in place for Northern Ireland from 12pm until 9pm today with warning of flooding and damage. Up to 30mm of rain could fall in an hour and there is also chance of hail.
Areas that do see a heavy downpour are at risk of flash flooding as scorched ground could cause significant water runoff.
It follows the driest July in England and Wales since records began. Parts of southern England may still not see a drop of rain, forecasters added.
Another record tumbled on Monday when the temperature reached 33.5C in Wisley in Surrey, marking the 20th day of 2026 when 32C or higher was recorded in the UK, exceeding the previous record of 19 days set in 1995, the Met Office said.
In the latest heat spike, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has amber heat health alerts in place for the East Midlands, East of England, South East and London until Wednesday morning.
There are also yellow heat health alerts for the North West, South West, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and The Humber, as the agency warns the latest high temperatures could put extra pressure on the NHS, with more vulnerable people likely to require medical treatment.
Outbreaks of rain and showers are forecast on Tuesday in Northern Ireland, Scotland, western England and Wales – but the Met Office has forecast a dry day for much of the Midlands, the east and south-east of England with warm sunshine and high humidity.
Temperatures are expected to decrease gradually in the second half of the week, and there is some more unsettled weather forecast for parts of the UK including a yellow warning for thunderstorms in Northern Ireland.
But the South East will continue to see little in the way of desperately needed rain, the Met Office has warned.
July was southern England’s driest month ever recorded, with the whole of Wales and half of England plunged into drought.
Farming leaders have warned it is “one of the most severe droughts many farmers and growers have lived through”, with poor yields, struggles to access water for fruit and vegetables and livestock keepers using winter feed for their animals.
The National Farmers’ Union (NFU) has demanded urgent action to secure water supplies for homegrown food production.
In July, 19 counties across England recorded effectively no rainfall – 1mm or less – across the whole of the month, the Met Office figures show.
The summer of extreme weather has seen two record-breaking heatwaves, in May and June, that led to more than 2,800 excess deaths, and two more heatwaves in July which have fuelled drought and wildfires.
Firefighters remained at the scene of a heathland blaze in Dunwich, Suffolk, on Monday, and crews declared a major incident as they tackled a huge wildfire in the Rhondda valley in South Wales.
Drone footage showed blackened ground and smoke billowing metres into the air over the valley, where South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) said the fire had affected 150 hectares of land, including forest, scrubland and vegetation.
What next?
The Met Office long range forecast says August will see a period of changeable weather, with initial forecasts predicting a mix of rain and showers alongside welcome drier interludes, particularly across the south.
As mid-August approaches, a significant shift in atmospheric pressure is anticipated. High pressure is expected to become more dominant across the north and northwest of the UK, while lower pressure systems may settle over southern and eastern regions. This pattern suggests an increased likelihood of frontal systems or thundery conditions affecting southern and eastern areas – a notable change compared to recent weeks. However, rainfall amounts are predicted to be quite variable, with some locations potentially experiencing relatively little precipitation.
Despite the unsettled outlook, temperatures are largely expected to remain above average, especially in the south, though without the exceptional heat witnessed recently.

Seoul and parts of Gyeonggi Province came under the capital region’s first Heat Wave Emergency Warning on Monday, as record-breaking heat in southeastern South Korea spread westward.
The Korea Meteorological Administration issued the warning at 4 p.m. for Tuesday, when the daily maximum perceived temperature is expected to exceed 38 degrees Celsius and the daytime high is forecast to surpass 39 C.
The warning, the highest level in the KMA’s heat alert system, applies to all Seoul districts south of the Han River, including Gangnam-gu, as well as Osan, Hanam and western Yeoju in Gyeonggi Province.
Introduced this year, the Heat Wave Emergency Warning signals exceptionally dangerous conditions in which even healthy people face a sharply increased risk of serious heat-related illness or death, KMA Administrator Lee Mi-seon said.
Under the warning, authorities strongly recommend suspending nonessential outdoor work and moving to air-conditioned indoor spaces or cooling shelters. They also advise stepped-up safety checks on vulnerable households.
The highest-level warning had previously been issued mainly in southeastern areas, particularly South Gyeongsang Province, after Yangsan recorded a national high of 42.5 C on Sunday.
The KMA attributed the westward spread of the heat to easterly winds carrying hot air toward the capital region.
High temperatures are also expected to persist overnight and in the coming days.
Article continues after this advertisement
“As heat accumulated during the day continues into the night, we urge residents in the metropolitan area to regularly check the latest weather information and take extra precautions, including staying hydrated and getting sufficient rest,” a KMA official said.

Extreme heat cancels two KBO games
The KBO called off Tuesday games in Seoul and Gwangju after the weather agency issued its highest-level heat wave warning.
Water is sprayed towards the LG Twins fans at the Jamsil Baseball Stadium in Songpa District, southern Seoul on July 29.
YONHAP
Two baseball games scheduled for Tuesday evening were canceled due to severe heat.
The KBO announced the game between the NC Dinos and the Doosan Bears in Seoul, and another between the KT Wiz and the Kia Tigers in Gwangju will not be played as earlier scheduled.
The Korea Meteorological Administration issued the highest-level heat wave warning for both cities earlier in the day.
The "serious" level heat wave warning is issued when the highest perceived temperature reaches at least 38 degrees Celcius (100 degrees Fahrenheit), or the maximum daily temperature reaches 39 degrees Celcius or higher. With the warning in place, the KBO may choose to cancel games by no later than 1 p.m. on a given day.
For Tuesday, the KBO made the announcement at 12:45 p.m.
Scorching conditions wiped out three KBO games in the southeastern region over the weekend — two in Changwon and one in Busan.
Of the three remaining games for Tuesday, one will be played in Busan and another will be contested in Daegu, which saw a record high temperature of 40.9 C on Sunday. The third game will be in Incheon, just west of Seoul.
Yonhap

The official said the Ministry of Finance (MoF) is maintaining a 2-percentage-point reduction in value-added tax (VAT) for goods and services subject to the standard 10% VAT rate, lowering it to 8% through the end of 2026.
| Deputy Minister of Finance Nguyen Duc Chi speaks at the Government's July press conference on August 3. |
The Government has also extended the exemption of agricultural land use tax until December 31, 2030 while allowing businesses and individuals to defer payments of VAT, corporate income tax and personal income tax during 2026.
In addition, a policy reducing or exempting 46 categories of fees and charges, starting July 1 last year, will remain in force until the end of this year to ease financial burdens on enterprises and households.
Highlighting the significant impact of fuel prices on inflation and economic activity, Chi said the MoF has proposed a series of tax measures to stabilize the domestic fuel market. These include cutting the preferential import tariff on fuel products and fuel production materials to 0% from March 9 to September 30, 2026.
The Government also reduced environmental protection tax, VAT and excise tax on fuel products to 0% between March 27 and June 30.
In addition, it has extended the application of a zero environmental protection tax rate on fuel products and fuel production materials until September 30. During the same period, businesses are exempt from declaring and paying VAT on these products while remaining eligible to claim input VAT credits.
According to the deputy minister, during the Middle East conflict, the state budget advanced 8 trillion VND (over 304 million USD) to the fuel price stabilization fund to help cushion domestic prices and maintain market stability.
The MoF is continuing to coordinate with the Ministry of Industry and Trade and other relevant agencies to develop contingency plans on pricing, taxes, fees and charges to respond to possible market disruptions. The measures are aimed at helping the Government maintain macroeconomic stability, keep inflation under control and ensure the achievement of the country's socio-economic development goals, Chi said.
